title: First Line of a Reel: 35 Ready-to-Film Hooks That Stop the Swipe

# First Line of a Reel: 35 Ready-to-Film Hooks That Stop the Swipe

At 8:43 p.m., your Reel is exported, captioned, and ready to post. The first line says, "Hey, today I want to show you..." By the time it reaches the useful part, a new viewer has swiped away.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/hIHxrr41KT.png)

If you searched for "first line of a reel," you need openings you can say on camera, not a lecture. These 35 examples give you a spoken first line, the on-screen text to pair with it, and a hook type to test. Use the examples as a starting point, then replace every bracketed detail with something you can prove on camera.

## Fitness and movement

**For:** beginners who want less intimidating workouts and clearer form cues.

1. **Spoken:** "Stop going to the gym every day."
   **On-screen:** Day 1 is where you quit
   **Type:** Contrarian
2. **Spoken:** "Your squat is not weak. Your first rep is."
   **On-screen:** Fix rep one first
   **Type:** Diagnosis
3. **Spoken:** "Beginners, do this before adding more weight."
   **On-screen:** Before you go heavier
   **Type:** Callout
4. **Spoken:** "I changed one warm-up and my knees stopped complaining."
   **On-screen:** The warm-up change
   **Type:** Result
5. **Spoken:** "If you quit by week two, your plan is too hard."
   **On-screen:** Week-two dropout fix
   **Type:** Stakes
6. **Spoken:** "This is what [ADD: your number] minutes of walking changed."
   **On-screen:** [ADD: your number] minutes a day
   **Type:** Result
7. **Spoken:** "Your plank is getting harder for the wrong reason."
   **On-screen:** The plank mistake
   **Type:** Curiosity

## Food and quick cooking

**For:** people who want dinner to work after a long day.

8. **Spoken:** "Your pasta is bland before it hits the sauce."
   **On-screen:** Fix this before the sauce
   **Type:** Diagnosis
9. **Spoken:** "Stop meal-prepping full meals. Prep this instead."
   **On-screen:** A better prep plan
   **Type:** Contrarian
10. **Spoken:** "If your chicken dries out, watch the pan first."
    **On-screen:** The pan is the problem
    **Type:** Callout
11. **Spoken:** "This dinner uses [ADD: your number] ingredients I already had."
    **On-screen:** [ADD: your number] ingredients, real dinner
    **Type:** Result
12. **Spoken:** "Do not add the garlic yet."
    **On-screen:** Garlic goes in later
    **Type:** Contrarian
13. **Spoken:** "The sauce split because of this ten-second move."
    **On-screen:** Why your sauce splits
    **Type:** Curiosity
14. **Spoken:** "Tired after work? Make this before ordering takeout."
    **On-screen:** A weeknight rescue
    **Type:** Callout

## Beauty and skincare

**For:** people whose routine has become crowded without becoming useful.

15. **Spoken:** "Your expensive serum may be doing nothing yet."
    **On-screen:** Do this before serum
    **Type:** Contrarian
16. **Spoken:** "If your makeup separates at noon, check this layer."
    **On-screen:** The layer that breaks makeup
    **Type:** Diagnosis
17. **Spoken:** "Sensitive skin? Test products here first."
    **On-screen:** Patch test spot
    **Type:** Callout
18. **Spoken:** "I stopped buying products for [ADD: your number] days."
    **On-screen:** What fewer products changed
    **Type:** Result
19. **Spoken:** "You are applying this product at the least useful time."
    **On-screen:** Timing matters here
    **Type:** Stakes
20. **Spoken:** "The order of your routine is fighting itself."
    **On-screen:** Your steps are out of order
    **Type:** Curiosity
21. **Spoken:** "Dry-skin people, do not skip this boring step."
    **On-screen:** The boring step that helps
    **Type:** Callout

## Small business and product videos

**For:** shop owners and solo operators who need a product clip to make sense fast.

22. **Spoken:** "Your product is not too expensive. It is too unclear."
    **On-screen:** Make the use case obvious
    **Type:** Contrarian
23. **Spoken:** "This is why people ask what you sell in the comments."
    **On-screen:** Your first shot is hiding it
    **Type:** Diagnosis
24. **Spoken:** "Small shop owners, show this before the pretty shot."
    **On-screen:** Start with the use case
    **Type:** Callout
25. **Spoken:** "This video brought [ADD: your number] product questions."
    **On-screen:** [ADD: your number] questions from one clip
    **Type:** Result
26. **Spoken:** "Do not lead with the packaging. Lead with this moment."
    **On-screen:** Show the problem first
    **Type:** Contrarian
27. **Spoken:** "The buyer needs to see this before the price."
    **On-screen:** Show this before price
    **Type:** Stakes
28. **Spoken:** "Watch what happens when the product leaves the shelf."
    **On-screen:** The product in real life
    **Type:** Curiosity

## Creator education and freelancing

**For:** creators and service providers whose useful advice keeps opening too politely.

29. **Spoken:** "Your Reel is not boring. Its first line is late."
    **On-screen:** The first line arrives too late
    **Type:** Diagnosis
30. **Spoken:** "If clients say yes too quickly, read this."
    **On-screen:** An instant yes is a clue
    **Type:** Stakes
31. **Spoken:** "Freelancers, stop explaining your service first."
    **On-screen:** Start with their stuck point
    **Type:** Callout
32. **Spoken:** "I cut [ADD: your number] words from this opening."
    **On-screen:** Shorter opening, clearer point
    **Type:** Result
33. **Spoken:** "More content ideas will not fix this empty calendar."
    **On-screen:** Ideas are not the problem
    **Type:** Contrarian
34. **Spoken:** "The first line of a Reel should answer this question."
    **On-screen:** Why should I stay?
    **Type:** Curiosity
35. **Spoken:** "Your tip is useful. The opening is hiding it."
    **On-screen:** Stop burying the good part
    **Type:** Diagnosis

## How to choose the first line of a Reel

Choose the line that makes a promise your next shot can begin proving. A contrarian line needs a real correction. A result line needs your own result. A callout needs to name a viewer you can help.

Read the spoken line aloud over the opening footage. If you need to rush it, cut it. If the overlay merely repeats every spoken word, shorten the overlay until it reads in a glance. If the line could sit over anyone's B-roll, add the object, mistake, or constraint that belongs to your Reel.

Keep the answer close. A first line earns a pause, then the next beat needs to reward it. Do not follow a sharp opening with a second introduction.

## How to test your first line

Write three openings for the same video: one diagnosis, one callout, and one result or contrarian angle. Film the body once and record only the first few seconds again for each version.

Post the versions separately under comparable conditions. In your platform analytics, compare the early retention shape, average watch time, and the comments that show whether the right people understood the promise. A dramatic line that holds attention but sends confused viewers into the comments is not a winner.

Keep a small note with the first spoken line, on-screen text, first frame, and the result. After several posts, you will see whether your audience stops for a visible mistake, a useful contrast, or a direct callout.


Related guide: [First line of a TikTok: 36 hooks that stop the swipe](https://aniccaai.com/blog/first-line-of-a-tiktok?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=related_links_1102b)

## FAQ

**How long should the first line of a Reel be?**

Keep it short enough to say naturally in roughly the first three seconds. Remove greetings, scene-setting, and any word the image already shows.

**Should the first line and on-screen text match?**

They should support the same promise, but they do not need to repeat each other. Let the text give a quick headline and let the spoken line carry the detail.

**Can I use a number in my hook?**

Yes, when it is your real number and the Reel can show what it means. Otherwise use a blank such as [ADD: your number] until you have a figure you can verify.

**What if none of my hooks feels right?**

Start with the footage. Find the first visible mistake, result, or surprising moment. Then write a line that tells the viewer why that frame matters.

## What the tool returns

Here is one published example of the input and the shortened output:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
